title: Mara and the Cellar
premise: Rosalind Ashgrove returns to the family farmhouse to bury her twin brother Rowan, whose body was found in the cellar with frost on his lungs in July. The imaginary friend of their childhood, a tall figure called the Latch, is waiting on the porch, unchanged after twenty years, and it insists Rosalind was always the one it wanted. As she uncovers the folk song their mother sang — a counting rhyme about children kept 'below the floor' — she learns Rowan survived by singing along, trading his voice and finally himself to keep the thing fed. To end it, Rosalind must learn the song's never-sung last verse from the thing's previous victims, who linger as frost-patterns on the cellar walls, without joining their chorus. In the climax she sings the verse alone, unmaking the bargain, and chooses to carry the truth home instead of the comfortable lie, burying Rowan a second time under his real name.
about_author: Wren Nystrom is the pen name of a former archivist of rural oral histories who grew up in farm country where cellars predate the houses above them. They write horror rooted in folk songs, family silence, and the things children know better than adults.

chapters.title: The Wrong Twin
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV. She arrives at the Ashgrove farmhouse for Rowan's funeral, numb with grief and an old guilt: everyone assumed she'd be the one to die young. The house smells of dust and something sweeter underneath. Emotional beat: dread disguised as mourning.

chapters.title: Porch Light
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV. At dusk she finds the Latch waiting on the porch steps — exactly as she drew him at age six, down to the too-long fingers. He says, 'You came back to me.' She slams the door and tells herself it was a hallucination. Emotional beat: the past refusing to stay buried.

chapters.title: Rowan's Room
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV. Sorting Rowan's belongings, she finds notebooks filled with the same line repeated for years: 'I sang so you wouldn't have to.' A cassette tape labeled 'for Roz, when I'm gone' resists every player she tries. Emotional beat: grief curdling into suspicion.

chapters.title: Mother's Rhyme
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV, with a memory interlude. She recalls their mother singing a counting rhyme about children 'kept below the floor' that always stopped before its final verse. In the kitchen she catches herself humming it and stops mid-note, heart hammering. Emotional beat: inherited fear surfacing.

chapters.title: The Funeral
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV. At the service, neighbors behave strangely — no one will look at the open casket, and old Mrs. Halloway grips her wrist and whispers, 'Don't sing at the graveside, whatever they ask.' The casket holds a body that looks like Rowan but isn't quite. Emotional beat: isolation; the town knows something.

chapters.title: Frost in July
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV. The coroner's report, obtained through a sympathetic deputy, lists cause of death as hypothermia — in midsummer — with frost crystals in the lungs. That night the temperature in the house drops around the cellar door. Emotional beat: rational explanations running out.

chapters.title: What the Latch Wants
chapters.summary: Latch's POV (first use). He has waited twenty years for Rosalind, the twin who stopped singing first. Rowan was a substitute, a lesser meal stretched thin. He is patient; he has been patient with this family for generations. Emotional beat: chilling tenderness.

chapters.title: The Tape
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV. An old reel-to-reel in the attic finally plays Rowan's tape: his voice, fraying, explaining the rules — never sing along, never answer when it uses your name, never go down alone. The recording ends with a second voice harmonizing. Emotional beat: posthumous plea.

chapters.title: Neighbors Who Remember
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV. Mrs. Halloway tells her about 1974, when three Ashgrove children went into the cellar and two came out singing. The survivor, Rosalind's aunt, spent her life in an institution drawing frost patterns. Emotional beat: the family curse made concrete.

chapters.title: Down the Stairs
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV. Against every rule, she descends into the cellar alone and finds the walls covered in frost ferns that move when she isn't looking directly at them. Each pattern, she realizes, contains a face. One of them is Rowan's. Emotional beat: awe and violation.

chapters.title: Voices in the Walls
chapters.summary: Multiple short POVs — the trapped victims speaking through the frost. They explain the bargain: the Latch keeps them 'safe' forever in exchange for their voices, sung nightly. There is a last verse to the song that frees them, but none can remember it, because remembering is what he takes first. Emotional beat: desperate hope.

chapters.title: The Aunt's Drawings
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV. Visiting the institution, she finds her aunt's decades of drawings: thousands of frost patterns, and hidden among them, notation — fragments of melody. Her aunt, lucid for one moment, says: 'He let me keep it because a broken verse is a better trap.' Emotional beat: bitter revelation.

chapters.title: Latch
chapters.summary: Latch's POV. He notices Rosalind gathering pieces and lets her — the incomplete verse is his favorite lure, the hope that draws singers close enough to harvest. He remembers her childhood clearly: how she gave him up willingly, and how he never forgave it. Emotional beat: predatory patience.

chapters.title: Assembling the Verse
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV. Cross-referencing the aunt's notation, Rowan's notebooks, and a 1911 hymnal from the church basement, she reconstructs most of the last verse. It is not a spell but a refusal — a naming of the dead that returns their voices. One line remains missing. Emotional beat: determined scholarship against time.

chapters.title: First Frost
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV. Frost appears indoors, writing patterns across windows and mirrors — the Latch accelerating, impatient now. The house grows colder each night. She finds her own name forming in the frost on her bedroom glass. Emotional beat: the deadline made visible.

chapters.title: Rowan's Bargain
chapters.summary: Rowan's POV (through the frost). Flashback chapters within: ten years ago Rowan discovered the Latch had chosen Rosalind and offered himself instead, singing the nightly chorus to keep her name off the list. His sacrifice bought her a decade. Emotional beat: devastating love.

chapters.title: The Missing Line
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV. The final line of the verse must be given freely by someone the Latch holds — spoken, not sung. She goes to the cellar to ask Rowan's frost-pattern, knowing the Latch will come. He does, offering her anything if she'll just sing one note with him. Emotional beat: temptation at its kindest.

chapters.title: One Note
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV. Alone in the dark, exhausted and grieving, she nearly sings — the harmony feels like coming home, like belonging. Rowan's pattern flares white across the wall, breaking the trance, and gives her the last line in a whisper: 'We were never yours to keep.' Emotional beat: loyalty vs. truth resolved.

chapters.title: The Last Verse
chapters.summary: Climax. Rosalind's POV. At dawn she stands in the cellar and sings the complete verse alone — naming every victim held in the walls, including the three from 1974 and her aunt's stolen sisters. The frost screams, the Latch unravels thread by thread as each named voice leaves him. Emotional beat: terrible, triumphant release.

chapters.title: Thaw
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV. The house warms. The frost patterns fade, leaving clean plaster and, briefly, the shapes of hands pressed in farewell. Rowan's presence lingers one moment — gratitude, then peace. The Latch is gone, or starved, or merely elsewhere. Emotional beat: grief finally allowed to be grief.

chapters.title: Second Burial
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV. She reburied Rowan under his full name with the true story read aloud over the grave, breaking the family tradition of silence. Neighbors begin telling their own truths. She sells the house but keeps the hymnal. Emotional beat: the price of survival paid forward as honesty.

chapters.title: Coda: The Song Without Its End
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV, years later. Teaching folklore to schoolchildren, she sings the counting rhyme but always stops before the last verse, which she has never written down. Some nights, in a new city far from any cellar, she hears humming three doors down — and chooses, again, not to answer. Emotional beat: survival as ongoing choice.
